title: Impulse changes momentum
lede: A force acting over a short time delivers an impulse, and that impulse is exactly the momentum change it produces.

cards.heading: Impulse
cards.body: Impulse is force times the time it acts, and it equals the momentum change it produces: J = F_avg * delta-t = delta-p. The average force during a brief collision is usually huge, because squeezing a fixed momentum change into a short contact time demands a large force. Car crumple zones work by stretching delta-t so F_avg drops.
cards.math: J = F_{\text{avg}} \, \Delta t = \Delta p = mv_f - mv_i

cards.heading: Momentum is a vector
cards.body: Momentum p = mv points along the velocity, so a rebound reverses its sign. The change is final minus initial with signs carried through — a ball bouncing off a wall can have nearly the same speed before and after yet a large momentum change. Forgetting the sign flip is the most common impulse mistake.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A 0.50 kg ball arrives at a wall moving right at 8.0 m/s and rebounds left at 6.0 m/s. Take right as positive: momentum goes from (0.50)(8.0) = +4.0 kg m/s to (0.50)(-6.0) = -3.0 kg m/s, a change of -7.0 kg m/s. If contact lasts 0.025 s, the average force is -7.0/0.025 = -280 N: 280 N pushing left, roughly 57 times the ball's 4.9 N weight.

flashcards.explain: Impulse measures the total push delivered by a force acting over a time interval. It equals the area under the force-versus-time graph, so a small force applied long can match a big force applied briefly.
The impulse delivered to an object equals its momentum change. The same momentum change squeezed into a shorter contact time demands a proportionally larger average force.
Momentum points along velocity, so a rebound flips its sign. Subtract initial from final without dropping signs: a head-on bounce gives a momentum change much larger than either momentum alone.

mcq.prompt: A 0.20 kg ball strikes a wall head-on at 15 m/s and rebounds at 10 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse the wall delivers to the ball?
mcq.rightExplain: Take the incoming direction as positive: delta-p = (0.20)(-10) - (0.20)(15) = -2.0 - 3.0 = -5.0 kg m/s, so the impulse magnitude is 5.0 kg m/s.
mcq.wrongExplain: 1.0 kg m/s subtracts the rebound momentum's magnitude from the incoming one, 2.0 kg m/s uses only the rebound momentum, and 3.0 kg m/s uses only the incoming momentum. All three miss the sign flip.

title: Momentum conservation and recoil
lede: Internal forces always cancel in pairs, so an isolated system's total momentum never changes — which is why cannons recoil and rockets fly.

cards.heading: When it holds
cards.body: Every internal force in a system has an equal and opposite partner (Newton's third law), so internal pushes shuffle momentum between parts of the system but never change the total. The total momentum of a system stays constant unless an outside force acts. Friction with the ground, gravity on a projectile, or a wall all count as outside.

cards.heading: Center of mass
cards.body: Total momentum equals total mass times the center-of-mass velocity. With no external force, the center of mass keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed no matter how violent the internal motion gets — an exploding shell's fragments scatter, but their center of mass traces the same arc the intact shell would have followed.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A 1200 kg cannon fires a 15 kg cannonball horizontally at 400 m/s. Total momentum before firing is zero, so after firing it must still be zero: the cannon recoils at (15)(400)/1200 = 5.0 m/s backward. Both objects gained kinetic energy — burning powder paid for it — yet the momentum still sums to zero.

flashcards.meaning: Total momentum of an isolated system is fixed
flashcards.explain: Internal forces cancel in pairs, so only external forces move the total. This holds in every collision and explosion, elastic or not, which is why it is the go-to bookkeeping tool.

Total momentum is total mass times center-of-mass velocity. With zero external force, the center of mass coasts: fragments of an explosion may fly everywhere, but their shared center keeps the original straight-line motion.
Add up every object's momentum before the event, watching signs, and the same total must appear after. Explosions start from zero total momentum, so the pieces' momenta must cancel.

mcq.prompt: A 40 kg child standing still on frictionless ice throws a 4.0 kg rock horizontally at 5.0 m/s. What is the child's recoil speed?
mcq.rightExplain: Total momentum starts at zero, so (4.0)(5.0) + (40)v = 0 gives v = -20/40 = -0.50 m/s: the child drifts backward at 0.50 m/s.
mcq.wrongExplain: 0.45 m/s divides by the combined 44 kg instead of the child's 40 kg, 5.0 m/s assumes the child flies off as fast as the rock, and 2.0 m/s divides the rock's momentum by the rock's own mass.

title: Elastic vs inelastic collisions
lede: Momentum survives every collision; kinetic energy only survives the elastic ones — and in one dimension elastic collisions have a clean shortcut.

cards.heading: Perfectly inelastic
cards.body: The extreme case: the objects stick together and share one final velocity. Momentum is still conserved even though kinetic energy is not — the missing energy went into denting, heating, and sound. Add the momenta before, divide by the combined mass after.

cards.heading: Elastic collisions
cards.body: An elastic collision conserves kinetic energy as well as momentum. In one dimension this gives a shortcut: the relative velocity reverses, so the closing speed before equals the separating speed after. Equal masses are a special case — they simply swap velocities, which is how billiards pass speed down the line.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: Inelastic: a 2.0 kg block sliding at 6.0 m/s hits a 4.0 kg block at rest and they stick. Final speed is 12/6 = 2.0 m/s; kinetic energy drops from 36 J to 12 J, so 24 J went into the crunch. Elastic: a 2.0 kg ball at 3.0 m/s elastically hits a 1.0 kg ball at rest; they separate at 1.0 m/s and 4.0 m/s, which conserves both momentum (6 = 2 + 4, in kg m/s) and kinetic energy (9 J = 1 J + 8 J).

flashcards.explain: When two objects fuse into one, divide the total incoming momentum by the total mass. This is the single most useful collision formula because so many real crashes approximate the stick-together case.

In a 1D elastic collision the relative velocity flips sign: the two objects separate exactly as fast as they approached. Paired with momentum conservation it solves any 1D elastic collision without square roots.

flashcards.meaning: Kinetic energy never increases in a collision
flashcards.explain: Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system, but kinetic energy survives only an elastic one. Real collisions sit in between, leaking some energy to heat and deformation. Explosions are the reverse: stored energy becomes kinetic, but momentum bookkeeping still balances.

mcq.prompt: A 3.0 kg block sliding at 8.0 m/s collides with a 5.0 kg block at rest and they stick together. What is their common speed after the collision?
mcq.rightExplain: Momentum is conserved: (3.0)(8.0) = (8.0)v', so v' = 24/8 = 3.0 m/s.
mcq.wrongExplain: 4.0 m/s averages the two speeds, 4.8 m/s divides the momentum by only the second block's 5.0 kg, and 8.0 m/s is the incoming speed unchanged — sticking to a heavier partner must slow the pair down.
